newsitem.title: CHINA: Rival Koreas in talks on food aid, deal elusive.
newsitem.headline: Rival Koreas in talks on food aid, deal elusive.

text.p: North and South Korea held another round of talks on Sunday aimed at clearing the way for grain shipments to famine-threatened Pyongyang but an accord appeared elusive.
The two cold war rivals, meeting in Beijing through their Red Cross societies, were holding working level discussions into the early evening, South Korean embassy officials said.
Food aid talks between Seoul and Pyongyang stalled on Saturday, partly over differences on the amount of grain to be shipped from South Korea, a South Korean embassy official said
North Korea has asked for 100,000 tonnes of food before the end of July while the South had offered to ship 40,000 tonnes.
"This is not possible," said a South Korean spokesman.
On Saturday, the two sides had still not reached agreement on how the aid should be shipped, through which ports it would travel and how it would be labelled, they said.
South Korean officials had previously said the talks could be completed on Sunday but that assessment appeared to be overoptimistic.
A news briefing scheduled by Seoul officials for Sunday was abruptly cancelled.

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean civil war ended only in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even basic food aid a delicate diplomatic affair.

Inter-Korean Red Cross talks earlier this month in Beijing failed after Seoul declined to say exactly how much aid it would supply to its Stalinist hermit neighbour, which aid workers say is facing widespread famine.

South Korea later promised to ship $8.0 million worth of corn, flour, powdered milk and instant noodles to the North by the end of July but details of how to transport, package and distribute the aid remained unresolved.

Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross delegation, had been pushing northern counterparts to accept direct transport through the town of Panmunjom on the highly militarised border between the two Koreas.

North Korea, which takes self-reliance as its guiding ideology, has sought to limit any direct contact involved in taking southern grain, while Seoul wants to maximise exchanges and to make sure its aid is clearly labelled as such.
Pyongyang had accepted that donated instant noodles would not be taken out of their labelled packets before distribution, but food labelled as coming from South Korea's Red Cross remained an issue.

While the aid pledged by South Korea is dwarfed by offers from other donors -- the European Commission said on Friday it was sending 155,000 tonnes of food -- it could lead to further shipments from the prosperous South.
